newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France to sell GAN, keep Thomson Multimedia.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France to sell GAN, keep Thomson Multimedia.

text.p: Going back on its tough anti-privatisation talk, France's new leftist government said on Friday it would go ahead with plans by its conservative predecessors to sell money-losing insurer GAN and its banking unit CIC.

But in line with last week's decision to reverse the sale of defence electronics giant Thomson-CSF, the government said its loss-making sister firm, consumer electronics firm Thomson Multimedia, would remain "a public company."

The late evening announcement came as the government cleared the decks for release on Monday of an audit of public finances expected to show a worsening of France's public deficit in 1997, the crucial qualifying year for European monetary union.

The Socialist-led coalition was seen as having little choice but to privatise GAN and its banking network CIC if it wanted to win European Commission approval to pump 20 billion francs into the insurer, hammered by a property slump in the early 1990s.
If it did not receive the Commission's assent, GAN had warned it could post 1996 losses of 14.7 billion francs.
After winning power on June 1, the government froze the conservative administration's plans to privatise a host of major companies aimed at making industry more competitive.
But facing a hole in its budget and battling to cut the deficit to qualify for monetary union, it has been softening up voters for a change of heart in the financial and other sectors.

Earlier on Friday, the government signalled it was prepared to sell a minority stake in France Telecom. The conservative government had planned to sell 35 percent of the telecoms operator, valued by analysts at 160-210 billion francs.
While the government cannot use privatisation proceeds to cut the public deficit, new cash can help it by allowing it to finance those firms needing capital injections.
The government said "commitments were taken leading to the privatisation of CIC and GAN" by the previous government and that it had "decided not to put into doubt these commitments."
At the same time, the finance ministry said it would seek ways to "limit the cost of the state's intervention."

The ministry said in a statement Thomson Multimedia (TMM), which like Thomson-CSF is part of state holding Thomson SA, also had asked the Commission to approve rapid state help. TMM is due to receive 10.87 billion francs in aid.

But the ministry said TMM would remain publicly owned, a solution which would strengthen an industrial group which has "remarkable assets." At the same time, strategic partners could be sought for the group over the longer term, it said.
The government said last Friday it would halt the sale of Thomson-CSF and would propose an alternative solution to build a French defence electronics conglomerate around the company.

At the same time, it said it was interested only in keeping a "decisive stake" in Europe's top defence electronics supplier, raising market hopes it might retain just a "golden share" to protect security interests rather than majority control.
Meanwhile, there are a variety of suitors for GAN, including rival French AGF, said to be considering taking over the insurer via a share swap, and Germany's Allianz.

The government scrapped an attempt last November to sell off GAN's profitable banking arm CIC after getting just one eligible offer. CIC was valued at around 14 billion francs in GAN's books which would correspond to around 9.4 billion francs for the 67 percent which the government put up for sale.
